threads.thread_goal: Align on churn definition, KPIs, and initial project scope.

messages.text: Kicking off the Customer Churn Prediction and Insights Dashboard project. Goal is to get aligned on what we mean by churn, the prediction horizon, and how we will measure success so we can move on T1 and T11. I have started a draft in A1 capturing a first pass at the problem statement and KPIs based on the brief. Proposal for discussion: 1) Churn definition: paying customer who cancels or does not renew their subscription within the next billing cycle. 2) Prediction horizon: 90 days ahead, so commercial teams have time to act. 3) Primary KPI: reduction in churn rate for contacted customers vs control; secondary: model precision/recall on high-risk band and incremental revenue saved. Can you review and react here so we can lock this in and reflect it in A8?

Thanks for framing this. On churn definition, do we want to include both explicit cancellations and silent non-renewals? Some teams only track explicit cancellations today. For prediction horizon, 90 days sounds reasonable, but sales mentioned they usually start renewal conversations around 60 days before end of term. Maybe we should clarify whether the 90-day horizon is relative to today or to contract end date. For KPIs, I would add a simple overall churn rate trend for the in-scope segment so stakeholders have a familiar metric in A1.

From a modelling side, it would help if we can translate the churn definition into a clear target flag in the dataset. For example, customer is marked as churned if they have no active subscription 90 days after a reference date. If we mix explicit cancellations and non-renewals, we just need to be sure the data sources can support that consistently. Once T3 starts, we will need this definition locked so we do not keep changing the label.

On the data side, I can check in T2 whether we can reliably distinguish explicit cancellations vs silent non-renewals across the subscription tables. In the first pass of the inventory for A2, I saw a status field and an end date, but I need to confirm how they behave in edge cases like downgrades. I will add notes in A1 once I validate this so the definition is grounded in what we can actually observe.

One question on the prediction horizon: if we go with 90 days, does that mean we will only train on customers whose outcome is known 90 days later? That might reduce the sample size. We could also consider 60 days if that aligns better with the renewal process. I can run some quick counts once T2 gives us the core tables, but I will need guidance from you on which horizon is more useful for the commercial teams.

Good points. Suggestion: 1) Churn definition: include both explicit cancellations and non-renewals, as long as the subscription is not active 90 days after contract end date. 2) Horizon: predict whether a currently active customer will be churned within the next 90 days relative to today, but we will also report metrics by time-to-contract-end in the dashboard later. This keeps the target clear for T3 while still matching how sales works. For KPIs, I agree to add overall churn rate trend as a headline metric in A1.

I am aligned with that proposal. To make it concrete for stakeholders, I will update A1 so it states: we predict whether an active customer will have no active subscription 90 days from today, based on cancellations or non-renewals. For KPIs, I will list: 1) overall churn rate for in-scope customers, 2) churn rate among contacted high-risk customers vs non-contacted, 3) revenue at risk vs revenue saved. These will also feed into A8 and T11 for the roadmap and communication plan.

With that clarified, for T4 and T5 we can use standard classification metrics aligned to the business KPIs. I suggest we track AUC, recall on the top risk band, and calibration plots, but we will translate them into business terms in A1 so non-technical readers understand. We should also agree on a minimum threshold for these metrics so we know when the MVP model is acceptable.

Before we lock the minimum thresholds, I would like to see the first baseline results in TH3. For now, can we agree that the primary business KPI is reduction in churn rate among customers flagged as high risk and contacted, and the secondary KPIs are overall churn rate trend and revenue saved? We can then map the technical metrics from T4 into these in A1.

I will make sure the data dictionary in A2 clearly flags which fields are used to derive the churn target and which are candidate features. That should help everyone see how the definition in A1 maps to the warehouse tables and will also support T3 later.
Yes, I am comfortable stating those as our KPIs in A1. I will also reflect them in the first version of A8 and T11 so stakeholders see how we will report impact in the bi-weekly updates.

Just to confirm, for the training dataset in T4 we will label a customer as churned if they have no active subscription 90 days after the reference date, regardless of whether it was a cancellation or non-renewal. I will rely on the flags and dates that T2 and A2 document. If this understanding is off, please correct me before I start building the first training script.

That matches the agreed definition. The only nuance is that the customer must be active at the reference date, which we will define as the snapshot date for each training example. I will add that wording into A1 so it is explicit.

On scope, I propose that for the MVP we focus on subscription customers with at least three months of history and exclude one-off transactional customers. This keeps T2 and T3 manageable within the 21-day deadline and matches the stakeholders who will use the dashboard first. I will document this scope and the out-of-scope items in A1.

Focusing on subscription customers with at least three months of history works for the modelling steps in T3 and T4. It will give us enough behavioural data to build features without stretching the timeline. We can revisit other segments in a later phase and add them to A8 as future roadmap items.

Great, then we have: 1) churn definition and 90-day horizon as described in A1, 2) primary and secondary KPIs agreed, and 3) MVP scope limited to subscription customers with at least three months of history. I will update A1 and A8 accordingly and reflect these in T11 so the roadmap and communication plan are consistent.

I will align the data inventory in A2 with that scope and tag the relevant tables and fields so it is clear what is in for the MVP. That will also help when we later extend the scope beyond subscriptions.

I will close T1 once the updates to A1 are done and share a short summary in the next stakeholder update using A8 as the base. That way everyone is aware of the agreed definitions and KPIs before we dive into data and modelling.

threads.thread_goal: Review data inventory and decide on data sources and quality fixes.

messages.text: I have uploaded the first version of the customer data inventory and quality report into A2 and linked it to T2. It covers the main customer, subscription, billing, and interaction tables from the warehouse. Key findings: 1) Subscription end dates are complete for 98 percent of records, but cancellation reasons are missing for about 40 percent. 2) Customer status is inconsistent between the CRM and billing tables for roughly 7 percent of customers. 3) Product hierarchy is not standardised across regions. We need to decide which sources we will use for the MVP and which data quality issues we must fix before T3.

Thanks for the summary. For the modelling dataset in T3, my initial thought is to rely primarily on the billing and subscription tables for the target and core features, and use CRM mainly for additional attributes like segment and region. The inconsistency in customer status between CRM and billing worries me a bit, since we need a clear definition of active customers for the target. Do you have a sense from A2 which system is closer to the truth for status?

From the checks in A2, billing seems more reliable for active vs inactive, especially around contract end dates. CRM sometimes lags by a few days. For the MVP, I suggest we treat billing as the source of truth for status and use CRM status only as a descriptive field. I can add a rule in the data quality notes in A2 to make this explicit.

Looking at A2, I noticed that interaction data from support tickets has some gaps before last year. For T4 and T5, it might still be useful to have recent support activity as a feature, even if the history is shorter. Do we want to include that table in scope for the MVP, or should we keep it for a later iteration once we clean it up more?

From a business perspective, recent support interactions are often a strong signal for churn, but given the 21-day timeline we should be careful. I would propose that for the MVP we include only the last 6 to 12 months of support data, where A2 shows better completeness, and we document the limitation in A1 and A3 later. That way T3 can still engineer a simple feature like number of tickets in the last 90 days without waiting for a full historical clean-up.

For the MVP scope, I suggest we prioritise: 1) billing and subscription tables as the backbone for target and revenue, 2) CRM for customer attributes like segment, region, and account owner, 3) recent support interactions as a limited feature set as just discussed. Marketing campaign data and product usage logs look more fragmented in A2, so I would keep them out of the first iteration and add them to the backlog in A8.

That matches what I am seeing in A2. Billing, subscription, CRM, and recent support data are in good enough shape for T3 with some targeted fixes. Marketing and detailed usage logs would need more work to be reliable. I will mark them as out of scope for T2 MVP and flag them as candidates for a phase two in the report.

On the quality issues, the two that seem most critical for T3 are: 1) the status inconsistency between CRM and billing, which we can handle by using billing as the reference as you suggested, and 2) the missing cancellation reasons. For the second, we might not need to fix all missing values before modelling, but we should at least ensure that missingness is not biased toward a specific segment. Could you add a quick breakdown of missing cancellation reasons by segment and region into A2?

Yes, I can extend the profiling in T2 to include that breakdown and update A2. If we see strong bias, we might decide to drop cancellation reason as a feature for the MVP and just keep a simple cancelled vs not flag derived from status and dates.

Given the selected sources, for T3 I will start drafting a simple schema for the model-ready table: one row per customer with joins to billing, subscription, CRM, and recent support aggregates. I will keep marketing and usage fields out for now, but leave placeholders in the script so we can add them later once the quality issues are addressed.

For prioritising fixes before modelling, I would rank them as: 1) align on active status using billing as the reference, 2) ensure subscription start and end dates are valid and non-null for in-scope customers, 3) basic standardisation of product hierarchy for the main product lines, 4) profiling of cancellation reason missingness as discussed. Other issues like minor CRM field inconsistencies can wait until after the MVP.

I agree with that ordering. It aligns with the business need to have a reliable view of who is active, when contracts end, and what they are buying. I will reflect these priorities in the risk section of A1 so stakeholders understand why we are focusing on these fixes first.

I will update T2 to explicitly call out those four priority fixes and mark them in A2. Once that is done, I will sync with the data platform owner to see if any of them can be addressed upstream rather than only in our pipeline.

Perfect. Once those fixes are in place, we can proceed with T3 using billing, subscription, CRM, and recent support as the in-scope sources for the MVP. I will document this selection in the data preparation notes so it is clear what feeds the model.

I will wait for the updated A2 with the priority fixes marked, then start implementing the joins and basic transformations for T3. I might need a quick check from you on some of the join keys if I run into inconsistencies.

threads.thread_goal: Discuss baseline model results and choose the model to take forward.

messages.text: I have run the first baseline models for T4 and logged the results in A5. Using the current T3 dataset with billing, subscription, CRM, and recent support aggregates, I tested: 1) a simple logistic regression, 2) a gradient boosting model. On the validation set, logistic regression achieved an AUC of around 0.71, while gradient boosting reached about 0.79. In the top 10 percent of customers by predicted risk, the gradient boosting model captures roughly 35 percent of observed churners. Calibration is reasonable but could be improved. I have added more details and plots in A3. We need to discuss what minimum performance we consider acceptable for the MVP and which model to take forward into T5 and the dashboard.

I went through A5 and noticed that the gradient boosting model is more complex to explain, especially around feature interactions. For A3 and for the commercial teams, do we think the gain from 0.71 to 0.79 AUC is worth the extra complexity, or should we aim for a simpler model first and then iterate?

From a business angle, the key question is how many churners we can surface in the high-risk band without overwhelming the teams. Capturing 35 percent of churners in the top 10 percent of customers is a good start, but we should also look at precision in that band. Do we have those numbers in A5? It would help to translate them into something like: if a sales rep calls 100 customers in the high-risk list, how many are likely to churn without intervention.

Yes, in A5 I added a table with precision by decile. For the gradient boosting model, in the top 10 percent risk band, precision is around 42 percent, meaning about 42 out of 100 flagged customers actually churned in the validation period. For logistic regression, precision in that band is closer to 30 percent. So the more complex model gives a noticeable lift in how focused the outreach list is.

Those numbers are promising. For the MVP, I would propose that our minimum bar is: 1) AUC of at least 0.75, 2) at least 30 percent of churners captured in the top 10 percent risk band, and 3) precision in that band above 35 percent. This would give us a clear story for stakeholders and aligns with the KPIs we defined in A1. Does anyone see a risk with setting these thresholds for D5?

Given the current results in A5, those thresholds seem achievable with the gradient boosting model. Logistic regression would not meet the AUC bar, so it would mainly serve as a benchmark and a simpler fallback. I do not see a major risk in adopting those numbers for the MVP, as long as we clearly document them in A3.

I am comfortable with those thresholds as well. They give us a concrete target while leaving room for improvement in T5. We should also make sure that the model is not overly dependent on any fields that might raise compliance questions, which we can cover in A3.

On the complexity vs benefit trade-off: while gradient boosting is more complex, we can still provide clear explanations using feature importance and partial dependence plots, which I have started to add to A3. The top drivers are contract tenure, recent support tickets, changes in subscription value, and product mix. We can translate these into simple narratives for the commercial teams.

Understood. If we can keep the explanations in A3 and the dashboard focused on those top drivers, I am fine with using gradient boosting for the MVP. For T5, I can also try a slightly simpler tree-based model to see if we can get close performance with fewer features, but that should not block the current decision.

For the stakeholder narrative, I will summarise in A1 and A8 that the model focuses on customers with certain patterns: shorter tenure, recent issues, and value changes. That should make the scores feel intuitive and help with adoption.

Given the discussion, I propose we formally adopt the gradient boosting model as the MVP candidate, since it meets the suggested thresholds in A5, and keep logistic regression as a benchmark. We will continue to log any new experiments in A5 under T5, but for integration with the dashboard we should focus on the current best model.

Agreed. For D6, let us confirm that the gradient boosting model is the one we will wire into the dashboard for the MVP, with the thresholds from D5 as the acceptance criteria. Please make sure A3 clearly documents the model version, training period, and key assumptions so we can share it with the compliance officer.

I will tag the selected gradient boosting run in A5 and store the model artefacts under T5 so we have a clear reference. I will also prepare a simple export of the scores and key features that the data analyst can use to start wiring T7.

I will update A3 with the finalised thresholds from D5 and the choice of gradient boosting for D6, including a short rationale comparing it to logistic regression. I will also add a section on limitations and next experiments planned under T5.

Once the export is ready, I will pull the scores and key features into the BI tool for T7 and start prototyping the main views. Please keep the field names consistent with the data dictionary in A2 so we avoid confusion later.

threads.thread_goal: Define churn risk bands, dashboard layout, and user journeys.

messages.text: I have drafted a proposal for churn risk segmentation and initial dashboard wireframes, linked to T6, T7, and T9. The details are in A4 and the layout checklist in A6. Summary: 1) Risk bands based on model score percentiles: high risk = top 10 percent, medium = next 20 percent, low = remaining 70 percent. 2) Main dashboard views: a) portfolio overview with counts and revenue at risk by band, b) account owner view listing their high and medium risk accounts, c) customer detail page with drivers and history. 3) User journeys: sales and customer success start in the portfolio view, filter by segment or region, then drill into their accounts. Please review and comment so we can refine and then sign off on thresholds and layout.

The structure in A4 and A6 looks solid. One question on the thresholds: given the model performance we agreed in TH3, do we want to keep high risk at 10 percent, or should we consider a slightly larger band, say 15 percent, to give teams more accounts to work with? It might depend on how many accounts each rep can realistically handle per week.

From the model side, the top 10 percent band is where we see the strongest lift in precision, as shown in A5. Extending to 15 percent would add more accounts but with lower precision. We could keep high risk at 10 percent and define medium risk as 10 to 30 percent, which still gives a sizeable pool for proactive outreach while keeping the highest urgency group focused.

On the dashboard layout for T7, the wireframes in A6 suggest a three-panel layout for the portfolio view: filters on the left, summary tiles on top, and a table below. That is feasible in our BI tool. For the account owner view, I would recommend adding a quick filter for account owner and a toggle to show only high risk vs high plus medium, so reps can adjust based on their capacity.

For the customer detail page, I can provide the top contributing features for each prediction from the model output, which you can surface as key drivers. We should probably limit it to the top 3 to 5 drivers to keep it readable. I will align the output format in T5 so it plugs easily into T7.

Given the precision numbers in A5 and the need to keep the list actionable, I lean toward keeping high risk at the top 10 percent and defining medium as 10 to 30 percent, as suggested. That gives us a clear story in A4 and T9: high risk for immediate outreach, medium for monitoring and lighter-touch actions, low for standard treatment.

I agree. Let us formalise the bands as: high = top 10 percent, medium = next 20 percent, low = remaining 70 percent, based on the model score distribution. In A4 we can also map recommended actions: for high risk, direct outreach and retention offers; for medium, check-in emails and monitoring; for low, no special action. This will feed directly into T9.

I will ensure the score output we generate for T7 includes both the raw probability and a pre-computed band label (high, medium, low) based on those thresholds. That will make it easier for the dashboard to filter and for A4 to stay consistent with the implementation.

On the user journeys, I suggest we add a simple onboarding banner in the dashboard that links to A4 and the playbook from T9, so new users can quickly understand what the bands mean and how to act on them. This can be a static text box in the portfolio view.

Good idea. I will incorporate that into the copy for A4 and the training materials in T9. The banner can highlight three key steps: review your high-risk accounts, prioritise by revenue at risk, and log actions taken so we can measure impact later.

For the layout sign-off, I would like to confirm that the three main views in A6 cover the core needs: 1) portfolio overview with filters for segment, region, and product line; 2) account owner view with their accounts and risk bands; 3) customer detail with drivers and history. If we agree, we can treat this as the first release scope for T7 and leave more advanced views, like cohort analysis, for later.

Yes, those three views are feasible within the timeline and align with what we discussed with stakeholders. I will start building them in T7 following the A6 checklist, including filters, drill-downs, and basic usability checks with two pilot users.

From the data side, I will make sure the export for T7 includes all fields needed for those three views: customer identifiers, risk score, band, revenue, segment, region, account owner, and the key driver fields. If anything is missing once you start building, let me know and I can adjust.

I am comfortable signing off on that layout for the first release. I will update A4 and A6 to reflect the final risk bands and views, and incorporate them into the training plan in T9. We can gather feedback from the pilot users and iterate in a second phase.

Great, then for D7 and D8 we have: 1) risk bands defined as high = top 10 percent, medium = next 20 percent, low = remaining 70 percent, with mapped actions in A4; 2) dashboard layout with the three main views in A6 approved for the MVP. Let us proceed with T7 and T9 based on this.

threads.thread_goal: Close out MVP, confirm monitoring plan, and plan training rollout.

messages.text: We are approaching the 21-day deadline, so let us review where we stand on the MVP and align on monitoring and training. A3 now has the updated model documentation, and A7 contains a first draft of the monitoring and data drift procedure linked to T8 and T10. A8 has the roadmap and communication plan. We need to confirm: 1) that the model and dashboard meet the agreed scope, 2) how we will monitor performance and data quality after go-live, and 3) the plan for training commercial teams using A4 and T9.

On the model side, T8 is nearly complete. A3 documents the methodology, features, training period, and the thresholds we agreed in TH3. For monitoring in T10, I propose we track: 1) monthly AUC and precision in the high-risk band, 2) churn rate among high-risk contacted vs non-contacted customers, 3) key feature distributions to detect data drift. These are outlined in A7, but I would like feedback before we finalise.

From the dashboard side, T7 and T12 are in good shape. The portfolio, account owner, and customer detail views are built, and the test refresh run for T12 completed without errors. The dashboard now updates daily with the latest scores, and I have documented the refresh schedule and dependencies in A7 and the monitoring notes.

For T10, I can implement the monitoring queries that compute the monthly AUC and precision metrics and log them to a simple table. We can then build a small monitoring view in the BI tool later if needed. I will also add checks for missing values and basic distribution shifts for the top features listed in A3 and A7.

On training and adoption, A4 and T9 now include a draft playbook and slide deck. The plan is: 1) run a 60-minute session with the pilot group from sales and customer success, 2) walk through the dashboard views and risk bands, 3) review example accounts and recommended actions, 4) agree on how they will log outreach so we can measure impact. I have pencilled this into A8 for next week, pending final confirmation that the dashboard is stable.

Great to hear the refresh is working. For T12, can you confirm that the dashboard reflects the latest model scores after each refresh and that there is a simple status indicator somewhere, so users know when the data was last updated?

Yes, the dashboard pulls from the latest score table after each daily refresh, and I have added a last updated timestamp at the top of the portfolio view. This is documented in the T12 notes and referenced in A7 so it is clear for monitoring.

Thanks. When you implement the monitoring queries for T10, please also include a simple alert rule as described in A7: if AUC drops below 0.7 or if the share of high-risk customers changes by more than 5 percentage points month over month, we should notify the data platform owner and the project channel.

Understood. I will add those thresholds into the monitoring scripts and set up email alerts to the data platform owner and this channel. I will document the process in A7 under T10 so it is clear who is responsible for responding to alerts.

For the business side of monitoring, I will work with the Head of Customer Success to define how we will track adoption: number of users accessing the dashboard, number of high-risk accounts with logged actions, and early signs of churn reduction in the pilot group. I will add these to A8 and reference A7 so they are part of the regular stakeholder updates.

On the training session, let us make sure we include a short section on limitations and responsible use, based on A3 and A4. For example, the model does not capture every possible churn driver, and scores should support, not replace, account knowledge. This will help manage expectations and support compliance.

Agreed. I will add a slide on limitations and responsible use to the T9 materials, drawing from A3 and A4. I will also include a section on how feedback from the pilot will be used to refine the model and dashboard, so teams see this as an ongoing collaboration.

Before we call the MVP ready, we should confirm that the compliance officer has reviewed A3 and A7. I have addressed the initial feedback on excluded sensitive features and documented the rationale. If there are any remaining concerns, we might need a quick sign-off meeting, but I believe the current documentation covers the main points.

I will share the latest versions of A3 and A7 with the compliance officer today and ask for a quick confirmation. Assuming no major issues, we can proceed with the pilot launch as planned in A8 and T9.

From a technical readiness perspective, I consider T7 and T12 done for the MVP: the dashboard is built, filters and drill-downs work, and the refresh process is stable. I will keep an eye on the first few days after go-live and log any issues in the project folder.

I will aim to complete the initial monitoring scripts for T10 by tomorrow and run a dry run using the latest data to ensure the metrics and alerts behave as expected. I will document the results in A7 so we have a baseline before the pilot starts.

Once we have confirmation from compliance and the monitoring dry run is done, I will schedule the pilot training session and send invites using the plan in A8. After the session, I will collect feedback and update A4 and T9 accordingly.

To summarise: 1) Model documentation and compliance notes in A3 are nearly complete under T8, pending final review. 2) Monitoring metrics and thresholds are defined in A7 and being implemented in T10, with T12 confirming the refresh process. 3) Dashboard and playbook are ready for the pilot, with training planned in T9 and A8. Unless compliance raises new issues, we are on track to launch the MVP pilot next week.
